questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Zeros of a Transformed Sine or Cosine Function
questions.problem: Which expression gives all of the zeros of $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{2})?$  Assume that $n$ is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's start by defining a new variable $X$ as

$$
X=2x+\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, we need to calculate the zeros of 

$$
y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡X.
$$

The zeros of this function are given by the following expression:

$$
X=n\pi 
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the zeros of our original function, we rewrite $X$ in terms of the original variable $x$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =n\pi  \\ 2x+\frac{\pi }{2} & =n\pi  \\ 2x & =-\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi  \\ x & =-\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{n\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the zeros are $x=-\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{n\pi }{2},$ where $n$ is any integer.

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Zeros of a Transformed Sine or Cosine Function

questions.knowledge_point: Exponential Functions With Vertical Reflections and Horizontal Shifts
questions.problem: Which of the following is the graph of $y=-{e}^{x}+5?$
questions.worked_solution:
To plot the given function, we follow these steps:

- We take the curve $y={e}^{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14006735/assets/f5983db4731c3fde0899ffc7afd602c7c82502f581742b62e69e8e6cf2d99e93.png)

 

- Reflect it on the $x$-axis to give $y=-{e}^{x}.$ The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,1)$ to $(0,-1)$ but the horizontal asymptote stays at $y=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14006735/assets/844a32e9d3640f9244b867c7411241171902c848defa0bf653b3820c3850238d.png)

 

- Then, vertically shift it by $5$ units up to give $y=-{e}^{x}+5.$ The point $(0,-1)$ moves to $(0,4)$ and the horizontal asymptote moves from from $y=0$ to $y=5.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14006735/assets/3303e36eb359692802a1c2184a2c54591f0b5de05853691841191a65689e8735.png)

The speed-time graph represents the motion of an object. Calculate the deceleration of the object.
questions.worked_solution:
The object is decelerating when its acceleration is negative. In a speed-time graph, the acceleration is given by the slope of the line.

The line passes through the points $(30,10)$ and $(50,5),$ so its slope is:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{5\text{ m/s}-10\text{ m/s}}{50\text{ s}-30\text{ s}} \\  & =-\frac{5\text{ m/s}}{20\text{ s}} \\  & =-0.25\,\frac{\text{m}}{{\text{s}}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration of the object is $-0.25\,\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ which means that the deceleration of the object is $0.25\,\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the LCM of Three Polynomials
questions.problem: Find the least common multiple of the polynomials $5(x-5)^{5}(y-2)^{3},$ $\,6(x-5)^{3}(y-2)^{3},$ and $12(x-5)^{3}(y-2)^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\text{LCM}$) of three polynomials that are made up of products of binomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of each variable part. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find $\text{LCM}(5,6,12):$

- Multiples of $5:$ $\,5,\,10,…,\,55,\,60,\,65,\,…$

- Multiples of $6:$ $\,6,\,12,…,\,54,\,60,\,66,…$

- Multiples of $12:$ $\,12,\,24,\,36,\,48,\,60,\,72,…$

So, $\text{LCM}(5,6,12)=60.$

To find the $\text{LCM}$ of $(x-5)^{5}(y-2)^{3},(x-5)^{3}(y-2)^{3},$ and $(x-5)^{3}(y-2)^{2},$ we find the largest powers for $(x-5)$ and $(y-2)$ that appear in all these expressions:

- For $(x-5)^{5},(x-5)^{3},$ and $(x-5)^{3},$ the largest power is $5.$

- For $(y-2)^{3},(y-2)^{3},$ and $(y-2)^{2},$ the largest power is $3.$

Now, we raise $(x-5)$ and $(y-2)$ to the corresponding largest powers. Therefore,

$$
\text{LCM}((x-5)^{5}(y-2)^{3},\,(x-5)^{3}(y-2)^{3},\,(x-5)^{3}(y-2)^{2})=(x-5)^{5}\cdot (y-2)^{3}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{LCM}(5(x-5)^{5}(y-2)^{3},\,6(x-5)^{3}(y-2)^{3},\,12(x-5)^{3}(y-2)^{2}) & = \\ 60\cdot (x-5)^{5}\cdot (y-2)^{3} & = \\ 60(x-5)^{5}(y-2)^{3} & .\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the LCM of Three Polynomials

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Area of a Quadrilateral
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14006735/assets/b0b100942a658966a5feea8a8677e7cfe86f21970a443385ff06034bbcb3d497.png)

Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD?$
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is the sum of the areas of the triangles $△ACD$ and $△ABC$ (see the illustration below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14006735/assets/7e3232258a523e4dbfebb6c380f5b88c2a54036b4d719e70ebf9060054f825d7.png)

 

First we find the area for $△ACD:$ 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ACD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 18\cdot 21\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘} \\  & =189\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘} \\  & ≈163.679,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Now we find the area for $△ABC:$ 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABC} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 36\cdot 30\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{33}^{∘} \\  & =540\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{33}^{∘} \\  & ≈294.105,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ACD}+{A}_{ABC} \\  & =163.679+294.105 \\  & =457.784\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $458.$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Area of a Quadrilateral

questions.knowledge_point: Completing the Square on an Expression With a Positive Leading Coefficient
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $3.$ So, we take out a factor of $3$ from the entire expression:

$$
3({q}^{2}-3q+5)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{q}^{2}-3q+5
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{q}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot q+5
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{3}{2})}^{2},$ writing the constant term $5$ last:

$$
{{q}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot q+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}_{⏟}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+5
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(q-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+5
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(q-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+\frac{11}{4}.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}3({q}^{2}-3q+5) & =3({(q-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+\frac{11}{4}) \\  & =3{(q-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+3\cdot \frac{11}{4} \\  & =3{(q-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+\frac{33}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Completing the Square on an Expression With a Positive Leading Coefficient

questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Variable Expression Containing a Quotient With Many Factorials
questions.problem: Given that $n\ge 0$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(n!)^{2}}{((n+1)!)^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we notice that

$$
(n+1)!=(n+1)n!
$$

Then, we can cancel the $n!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n!)^{2}}{((n+1)!)^{2}} & =\frac{n!\cdot n!}{(n+1)!\cdot (n+1)!} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{n!}\cdot \cancel{n!}}{(n+1)\cdot \cancel{n!}\cdot (n+1)\cdot \cancel{n!}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(n+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Simplifying a Variable Expression Containing a Quotient With Many Factorials

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Sum Containing a Natural Logarithm Function
questions.problem:
Given the function  $y=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{e}^{x}$, find the instantaneous rate of change at $x=1.$ Do not round the answer.

The instantaneous rate of change at $x=1$ is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the instantaneous rate of change at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{2}{x}+{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(\frac{2}{x}+{e}^{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{2}{1}+{e}^{1} \\  & =2+e\,.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Differentiating a Sum Containing a Natural Logarithm Function

questions.knowledge_point: Adding and Subtracting a Number and a Rational Expression
questions.worked_solution:
Using the fact that $4=\frac{4}{1},$ we can write the expression as

$$
\frac{4}{1}+\frac{4}{n}.
$$

 

In order to add the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. So, we put both fractions over a common denominator of $n$ by multiplying the top and bottom of the first fraction by $n:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{1}+\frac{4}{n} & = \\ \frac{n}{n}\cdot \frac{4}{1}+\frac{4}{n} & = \\ \frac{4n}{n}+\frac{4}{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we add the fractions and simplify the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4n}{n}+\frac{4}{n} & = \\ \frac{4n+4}{n} & = \\ \frac{4(n+1)}{n}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Adding and Subtracting a Number and a Rational Expression

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Horizontal Stretch and Vertical Shift of a Transformed Cotangent Curve
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14006735/assets/c9ed24a7fa07d6c29e4125c8428fb61a42fc969b99f101c4737bdedf9bf036ff.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(Bx)+D,$ where $B$ and $D$ are constants. What is $B+D?$
questions.worked_solution:
The period $T$ of the function is

$$
T=\frac{4\pi }{3}-0=\frac{4\pi }{3}.
$$

The formula for the period $T$ of the function $y=A\operatorname{cot}⁡(Bx+C)+D$ is given by 

$$
T=\frac{\pi }{B}.
$$

Applying the formula of the period, we get

$$
\frac{4\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{B}\,⟹\,B=\frac{\pi }{(\frac{4\pi }{3})}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

The parameter $D$ represents the vertical shift of the cotangent function. We see that the function has been translated by $3$ units down. Hence, $D=-3.$

Therefore, $B+D=\frac{3}{4}+(-3)=-\frac{9}{4}.$

Finally, the equation of the curve is

$$
y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3x}{4})-3.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Identifying the Horizontal Stretch and Vertical Shift of a Transformed Cotangent Curve
